title: “Devoid of Any Factual Basis”: Again and Again, Judges Have Dismissed Trump’s Voter Data Lawsuits
author: Peter Elkind
content:
Since September 2025, the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division has
sued**** 30 states and the District of Columbia to demand their unredacted
voter rolls.

![A cartogram of the United States shows 30 states and the District of
Columbia highlighted in green.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261014_dojVoterRolls_an_1.jpg?w=752)

The rolls contain confidential information on millions of Americans and have
historically been managed by states. Now these lists are a major focus of
President Donald Trump’s push to take federal control over elections and
prosecute alleged noncitizen voters.

To date, there have been final rulings in 26 of the DOJ lawsuits.

Four cases are yet to be decided, and one state settled.

![A cartogram of the United States shows 26 states and the District of
Columbia highlighted in green, indicating final rulings in those lawsuits.
Four states have a hatch pattern, indicating the cases are yet to be decided.
One state, Oklahoma, is dark gray, indicating the case has
settled.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261014_dojVoterRolls_an_2.jpg?w=752)

Of the judges randomly assigned to the 26 cases, eight were Trump appointees,
four were appointed by another Republican — George W. Bush — and 14 were
appointed by Democrats.

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261015_dojVoterRolls_an_3.jpg?w=752)

### **Tactic No. 1**

The first seven lawsuits used the same opening, citing Trump’s March 2025
executive order on election integrity to claim the Justice Department needed
states’ voter rolls to check that they were following federal election laws.

_“The United States’ championing of its claims under the [election laws], in
both its briefing and its presentation at the hearing on this matter, can only
be described as halfhearted. And for good reason, since neither statute gives
the United States the power to compel Maine to produce its current [unredacted
voter list].”_

—Maine federal Judge Lance E. Walker (Trump appointee)

The judges ruled that there was no legal or factual basis for the government’s
demand. They noted that the laws require states to keep accurate, up-to-date
computerized voter lists that include confidential information. But the
statutes give the federal government limited power to enforce those mandates.

Several judges accused the administration of using the election laws as a
pretext to suppress voting.

_“The foundation upon which American democracy has been built is the right to
vote. … Now it seems the Executive Branch of the United States government
wants to abridge the right of many Americans to cast their ballots. … The
Court does not take lightly DOJ’s obfuscation of its true motives.”_

—California federal Judge David O. Carter (Bill Clinton appointee)

_“Public statements from government officials reveal its intentions: to create
a nationwide voter-database, for potential weaponization in future elections;
as a ‘fishing expedition,’ hoped to advance unsubstantiated claims of non
citizen voting; and as a tool for immigration enforcement.”_  

—Pennsylvania federal Judge Cathy Bissoon (Barack Obama appointee)

In an extraordinary rebuke ([echoed by other courts around the
country](https://www.propublica.org/article/justice-department-presumption-of-
regularity)), the judge hearing the Oregon case wrote that the federal
government’s actions undermined the judiciary’s longstanding trust in the
Justice Department. He called them “chilling.”

_“The presumption of regularity that has been previously extended to Plaintiff
that it could be taken at its word — with little doubt about its intentions
and stated purposes — no longer holds.”_

—Oregon federal Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai (Joe Biden appointee)

All seven lawsuits using the first tactic were dismissed.

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261015_dojVoterRolls_an_4.jpg?w=752)

### **Tactic No. 2**

The next 19 lawsuits used a different strategy.

They made no mention of Trump’s executive order and didn’t depend on federal
voting laws. Instead, they cited a provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1960
called Title III, which requires the preservation of state and local election
records.

The government lawyers claimed that Title III gave the attorney general
“sweeping power” to obtain these records to curb noncitizen voting. In
reality, the law allowed the federal government to access such records to
protect the right to vote, for example, by enabling investigations into
practices that disenfranchised Black voters in the South.

Judges rejected the government’s arguments, ruling that Title III applies only
to voter registration documents, not records that states generate themselves,
like voter rolls. They noted the government had also failed to give an
explanation of why it needed the records, as the statute requires.

_“Clearly, this demand is devoid of any factual basis.”_

—West Virginia federal Judge Thomas E. Johnston (George W. Bush appointee)

Several judges marveled at the audacity of the administration’s attempt to use
an anti-discrimination law to keep people from voting and condemned the
administration’s logic.

_“Title III was the Department of Justice’s answer to two years of resistance
and obstruction by state election officials who destroyed, failed to retain,
or simply refused to disclose the voting records … that would prove that black
voters were victims of disparate treatment and had been unlawfully excluded
from the rolls based on nothing more than their race.”_

—D.C. federal Judge Randolph D. Moss (Obama appointee)

Judges also noted that there was a conflict between the DOJ’s claim to be
enforcing election laws, which require voter lists to be continuously updated,
and Title III, which bans any alteration of voter records.

_“The United States’s proposed interpretation of the CRA would therefore
criminalize the same conduct that the [voting laws] require. This Court will
not read [Title III] to produce such an absurd result.”_

—Maryland Judge Stephanie A. Gallagher (Trump appointee)

The administration’s interpretation of Title III, wrote Bissoon, the
Pennsylvania judge, “does violence” to the law’s meaning.

To date, judges have dismissed 19 DOJ complaints that relied on the Civil
Rights Act claim.

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261015_dojVoterRolls_an_5.jpg?w=752)

In written opinions, every one of the 26 judges has rejected the Justice
Department’s arguments and thrown out its lawsuits. Four cases are still
ongoing.  

The Trump administration has appealed most of its losses to federal appeals
courts and has said it will consider taking its fight to the Supreme Court.

A Justice Department spokesperson issued a statement in response to
ProPublica’s questions: “Our attorneys are skilled, principled advocates who
argue every case honestly and in good faith. Disagreement with the
government’s position is not evidence of bad faith. We look forward to making
our case on appeal.”

The only appeal decided so far backed the district judge who threw out the
Michigan case.

_“Back then, the government used this power to ensure that everyone who had
the right to vote could freely exercise that right. But today, the government
invokes Title III for an inverse purpose — to ensure that some people have not
voted.”_

—Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals opinion

On Oct. 9, a U.S. district judge ruled that the Justice Department’s national
effort to acquire and share state voter rolls was an illegal abuse of its
authority. A Justice Department spokesperson said the department is “reviewing
the ruling.”
